name: git status
shortDescription: Show the working tree status. Displays which files are staged, modified, untracked, or conflicted — your go-to command for understanding the current state of the repository.
detailedDescription:
The `git status` command is your dashboard. It answers the most common question in Git: 'What is going on in my repository right now?' It shows three categories of information:

1. **Changes to be committed** (staged) — files that are in the staging area and will be included in the next commit.
2. **Changes not staged for commit** (modified) — tracked files that have been modified but not yet staged.
3. **Untracked files** — files that exist in the directory but are not tracked by Git.

Git also shows the current branch, whether it's ahead or behind its upstream, and any ongoing operations (merge, rebase, cherry-pick). Running `git status` is always safe — it never modifies anything.

During a merge conflict, `git status` becomes critical: it shows which files have conflicts that need resolving (listed under 'both modified').

parameters.description: Give output in a compact two-column format. The left column shows the staging status and the right column shows the working directory status. M = modified, A = added, D = deleted, ?? = untracked, U = unmerged.
Show the branch and tracking info even in short format. Adds a header line like `## main...origin/main [ahead 2]`.
Machine-readable output format that is guaranteed to be stable across Git versions. Ideal for scripting and automation.
Also show files that are being ignored by .gitignore rules. Useful for debugging why a file isn't appearing.

examples.title: Check repository state (everyday usage)
examples.description: Run this before and after every git add and git commit to understand what's happening.
examples.code:
git status

# Typical output:
# On branch main
# Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
#
# Changes to be committed:
#   (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
#         modified:   src/app.js
#
# Changes not staged for commit:
#         modified:   src/style.css
#
# Untracked files:
#         src/new-component.js

examples.title: Short format for quick scanning
examples.description: When you know what you're looking for, the short format is much faster to read. Each file gets a two-letter status code.
examples.code:
git status -s

# Output:
# M  src/app.js          ← staged modification
#  M src/style.css       ← unstaged modification
# ?? src/new-component.js ← untracked file
# A  src/utils.js        ← staged new file
# D  src/old.js          ← staged deletion

examples.title: Check branch tracking status
examples.description: See if your local branch is ahead of, behind, or diverged from the remote.
examples.code:
git status -sb

# Output:
# ## main...origin/main [ahead 3, behind 1]
#  M src/style.css

# This tells you: you have 3 local commits not pushed,
# and the remote has 1 commit you haven't pulled.

examples.title: Debug .gitignore issues
examples.description: If a file that should be ignored is showing up (or vice versa), use --ignored to see what Git is ignoring.
examples.code:
git status --ignored

# Shows a section:
# Ignored files:
#   (use "git add -f <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
#         node_modules/
#         .env
#         dist/

commonMistakes.text: Run `git status` constantly. Before staging, after staging, before committing, after pulling. It's the safest command in Git and is your primary debugging tool.
If `git status` shows files you don't want tracked, add them to `.gitignore`. But if they're already tracked, you must also run `git rm --cached <file>` to stop tracking them.
Use the short format (`-sb`) in your shell prompt via tools like `oh-my-zsh` or `starship` to always see your Git status without typing the command.
